This isn\'t the workshop; this exercise is for examiners.
Intro

By compiling and launching the app, you\'ll get access to the exercise titles. You\'ll be able to see the Expected mockup and the Exercise result, the result you\'ll build yourself as the workshop progresses.
Welcome
It\'s your first day at the CIA, a new adventure starts here. Throughout this workshop, you\'ll encounter tools that Jetpack Compose provides to build the most beautiful apps in Kotlin.
Jetpack Compose

With Jetpack Compose everything is "Composable" and a Composable is a Kotlin function that carries the @Composable annotation. You can make it configurable with parameters passed when calling this function.
First Hello World

One of the simplest Composables provided by Jetpack Compose is Text. To start your initiation, what could be better than making a nice Hello World\u00A0? Go to the indicated file and add the following code\u00A0:
Preview
You may have noticed it isn\'t easy to see your code changes immediately in your app… You have to relaunch the app and it can take time…

Most of the time, we recommend that you first build your Composables without leaving the IDE, using what we call a Preview. It lets you see the Composable on its own before integrating it into a screen.

To do this, under the ExerciseHelloWorld Composable, create a Composable named ExerciseHelloWorldPreview and annotate it @Preview. You can even make it private since it has no reason to exist outside this file.
In the IDE
Your Previews are available in the Split tab at the top right of your file.
Live update
There is another mechanism called Live Update. It lets you see changes live directly in the app while editing your Composables.
Although this tool looks promising, it has a few limits. Live Update doesn\'t detect all changes, so you\'ll sometimes need to relaunch the app to see your progress.
Scaffold
We\'ll now create a structured screen to integrate our Composables. You can easily imagine a screen made of a topBar, a bottomBar and a central content.
In Jetpack Compose, you can create this structure thanks to the Scaffold Composable. Try adding it.
TopBar
To display a centered title, we can use the CenterAlignedTopAppBar Composable.
Add it in the topBar = { … } parameter of the Scaffold\u00A0:
BottomBar
Likewise, use the bottomBar = { … } field to show a simple "Badge" text at the bottom of the page.
Android Studio should warn you about a missing piece, move on…
Edit
Add the "Hello World!" text from the previous exercise into the Scaffold content.
Done and you don\'t see it appear in the app\u00A0? That\'s normal\u00A0!

Material\'s Scaffold doesn\'t force you to show the content below the TopBar; that can be handy if you want content that can scroll under the TopBar, for example. Scaffold therefore provides values so you can draw content between the TopBar and BottomBar, and it is warning you that you haven\'t used those values yet.

To position the content, we\'ll use its modifier argument. Every Composable has one; we\'ll pass modifiers to change the element\'s appearance or behavior. This generic parameter adds to the specific parameters offered by each Composable.

Use the paddingValues parameter that Scaffold provides, and pass it to the content\'s Modifier padding. This adds margins above and below the content so it doesn\'t overflow under the TopBar or BottomBar.
You should now see your content\u00A0!
Center the content
The content ends up at the top-left of the screen; that\'s its default behavior. Without contrary instructions, it positions itself there using as little space as possible.
To center it, we\'ll wrap it in a Box that we\'ll stretch to take all the space it can access (remember the margins from the Scaffold), then we\'ll ask the Box to center its content.
Careful: now that the Text is no longer the direct child of the Scaffold, it\'s no longer the one that should take the paddingValues; it\'s the Box.
Text appearance

Let\'s move to the BottomBar text; it doesn\'t deserve to be so visible. Use its "style" field to set its appearance. Material provides a set of "typography" to add meaning to our texts; use MaterialTheme.typography.labelMedium.
Once the style is set, add a bit of margin around it, 4dp (density-independent pixels) should be enough\u00A0:
Note\u00A0: Scaffold is often used to lay out screens but more rarely to lay out their content.
Layout
But who are you\u00A0? This info should be on your badge. Let\'s say it would look good to have a photo as well as your first and last name.
Simpler than Scaffold, we\'ll use a Column here. As you might expect, this composable displays its children in a column, one below the other.
To start, don\'t show an image but simply the word "Image".
On a first line, show the word "Image" then, on a second, show your first and last name.
Alignment
As always, by default composables try to align to the left. To center them, Column provides a horizontalAlignment parameter.
To control their vertical positioning, Column provides another parameter\u00A0: verticalArrangement. Here we just want a bit of space between each child; 4dp should be enough.
Note\u00A0:Row provides the opposite parameters: verticalAlignment and horizontalArrangement.
Your profile is ready to be integrated into your badge. Simply replace the old "Hello World!" with the CIAProfile() composable you just coded.
Image
You can\'t walk the halls with the word "Image" on your badge, that makes no sense\u00A0!
So replace this text with the Image composable. It will make your badge more visual, more relevant. But don\'t show your photo; at the CIA we use avatars to blur our identity.
Accessing resources

Images are part of resources called "drawables" in Jetpack Compose. You can use them by providing a "painter resource" to the Image composable. Choose the right image among avatar_blue, avatar_orange and avatar_red.
Accessibility is an important topic for Jetpack Compose; when you use an image, you must provide a text alternative via the "contentDescription" parameter.
Note\u00A0: This Composable can display PNG, JPEG, WEBP images, as well as vector images in AVD (Android Vector Drawable) format, inspired by SVG.
Clip an image
Based on the code you produced in the previous exercise, we\'ll try to improve the visual rendering of your avatar.
Apply a clip Modifier to the avatar composable to change its shape. A CircleShape clip will round the avatar.
Note\u00A0: As you can guess, you can apply this behavior to any Modifier, which means you can round the corners of any Composable\u00A0!
User interaction
The basic mobile interaction is tap; it\'s known as "click" in Jetpack Compose. You\'ll find it under several forms like "onClick" or "clickable".
To make your badge interactive, reuse the code previously written.
Managing a variable
Here, we want to vary the size of the 4 corners of our image. We\'ll create a variable that remembers that size.

In Jetpack Compose, variables are wrapped in remember; think of them as memoization. We\'ll also ask this variable to impact what we show on screen. To do that, we must declare it as a "mutable state".
The variable corner is initialized to 0 and may change.
Changing the clip
Do you see how to vary the clip shape based on another shape than CircleShape?
Didn\'t find it? What about RoundedCornerShape\u00A0?
If you look at your work, the image is now square again. For it to become round, our variable corner must be equal to 50.
Clickable
Look in the docs for the Modifier that lets you define behavior to react to a click on the image.
So try changing the value of our variable to play with the image\'s shape.
You can now see the interactive image from your preview!
Your avatar is ready to be integrated into your badge. Simply replace the old "image" text with the CIAImage() composable you just coded.
Skills
Well… besides building apps in Compose, you might have other skills, right\u00A0? Why not show them proudly on your badge\u00A0? Let\'s find some space under your profile.
Let\'s start by designing a CIASkill Composable that can display a given skill. Then, if that Composable is configurable, we can reuse it to show your full palette of talents.
To highlight it a bit, use the Material design system\'s Card Composable. As its name suggests, it shows its content as a card, as if you laid it on the screen.
Parameters
Use your previous lessons to build the rest of CIASkill. The new thing will be the use of parameters passed to the Composable to make it configurable.

Here is the id of the image to use along with a few keywords that can help you\u00A0:
Highlight

You surely have a particular skill, that little something that sets you apart from your colleagues. How about highlighting it on your badge? Something like a small star on the right of the skill Card.

It\'s time to discover another composable that draws an image, more precisely an icon. The difference here is that an icon could be seen as a shape rather than a drawing. The Icon composable is a lot like Image and offers an easy way to apply a tint.
Little tip: Material gives you a set of icons where you\'ll surely find what you need\u00A0: Icons.Default.Star.
You can conditionally display this composable based on the isBest parameter passed to the CIASkill composable.
Note\u00A0: Don\'t hesitate to use auto-completion when browsing Material Icons.
Stretch an element
You may have noticed that the icon isn\'t automatically stuck to the right of the Row. Once again, by default, composables try to position themselves as far left as possible.
There are several ways to address this; here we\'ll ask the texts to stretch horizontally.
As soon as a composable is inside a Row, you can apply a Modifier .weight(1f) and then ask it to take as much space as possible without stepping on its neighbors.
It\'s time to add your skills to your badge. We could make some room under your first and last name.
Column was made to show Composables one below the other, you might think it\'s the one to use here.
Nope\u00A0! Each exercise is a chance to discover something new.
LazyColumn
LazyColumn is a Composable we often use to display a large list of items that would require the user to scroll to see all of them.

This would consume too many resources to compute hundreds of items the user won\'t see before scrolling. Phones aren\'t made to handle that much information, so LazyColumn only computes items on screen and delays computation of the next ones.
A small usage difference: you don\'t give Composables directly to a LazyColumn. You give it item { … } blocks inside which you define your Composables.
Note\u00A0: LazyColumn also practices composable recycling by reusing those that disappeared on one side to display those that appear on the other.
Integration
Add 2 skills to your badge using a LazyColumn.
Two screens
We\'re getting to the last exercises of this workshop. Congrats on making it this far, you\'re almost ready to go out in the field!
Before moving to the final exercise, you\'ll prepare the back of your badge by setting up navigation to go from one side to the other.
NavigationBar
To model the front and back of your badge, we\'ll use a NavigationBar. It will be composed of 2 NavigationBarItem named "BADGE" and "MISSIONS".
Install this NavigationBar in the Scaffold\'s "bottomBar". That\'s usually where navigation elements live.
Current page
Use this variable to know which NavigationBarItem is currently selected.
Also remember to update this variable when one of the NavigationBarItem is clicked.
From one side to the other
For now, we\'ll just simulate the page change.
To do this, use the currentPage variable in a Text present in the Scaffold content.
Front
Reuse the previous exercise to lay out your badge.
Then replace the text simulating the pages with a condition. If currentPage is 0, then show the CIAIdentity Composable. If it\'s 1, then show a text "Mission list".
